excerpt: Can an LLM Grade Objective Facts Without Favoring Itself? Most evidence of self-preference in LLM-as-a-judge setups comes from open-ended tasks like chat, summarization, and creative writing. In those settings, a model favoring its own family is easy to explain away as stylistic taste or lower token perplexity. Standard evaluation guides offer a straightforward fix: use reference-based grading. Give the judge a verbatim quote from the source text, an explicit answer key, and an anonymized ID with no model metadata, and it ought to behave like a neutral referee. We tested whether that holds up in practice. Using a 123-question closed-book testbed built from technical standards, we ran three frontier model families (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Astra, and Gemini 4 Carbon) and had all three grade all 366 answers blind through the exact same single-shot API script. The results were not uniform across model families. Even with the literal spec text sitting inside the grading prompt and all model names stripped out, GPT-6.2 Astra still graded its own answers 5.8 to 7.0 points higher than its strictness on other models predicts (p = 0.003 to 0.012). Meanwhile, Gemini 4 Carbon showed virtually zero self-preference (+0.2 to +0.8 points). That divergence is wide enough to flip #1 and #2 on the leaderboard depending on which family sits in the judge’s chair. 1. The Testbed: Objective Specs, Gray-Zone Answers# To test whether reference-grounded grading eliminates bias, we needed questions with unambiguous ground truth that still push frontier models into borderline mistakes. Technical standards are ideal for this: every rule is written down, yet subtle version changes and release-specific quirks trip models up constantly. The question bank. 123 closed-book questions anchored to verbatim clauses across six technical domains, verified by script against the source texts and split across four question types: Answering.
